tier_reason: TCHES 2022 paper (author's PDF copy) with a public artifact repo: microbenchmark harness dilithium3/microbenchmarks/speed.c (PMU cycle counter, gcc 10.3.0 -O3), m1_benchmarks/dilithium_speed.c (Apple clang 12.0.5 -O3) and full-scheme runs through public SUPERCOP 20210604, on a Raspberry Pi 4 (Cortex-A72 at 1.5 GHz) and an Apple M1 Mac mini; every claimed number matches Tables 4, 5 and 6 and the paper's prose. Reference rows of Tables 4-5 have no harness in the repo, but Table 6 reference rows are reproducible through SUPERCOP.

corrections.caveats: The Dilithium baseline is the unoptimised portable reference code, so the 4-8x kernel gains largely measure hand vectorisation against scalar C; the Kyber and Saber comparisons are against another Neon implementation (Nguyen-Gaj, intrinsics), where gains are roughly 1.1-2.1x. The paper notes the Nguyen-Gaj NTT cycle counts omit the final reduction. Cortex-A72 numbers are medians (10 000 runs; 100 000 for full Dilithium), Apple M1 numbers are averages (10 000 runs; 1 000 000 for full Dilithium). Full-scheme ratios mix NTT and hashing gains: the optimised builds use a two-way Neon SHA-3/SHAKE (Nguyen et al.) on Cortex-A72 and Westerbaan's Keccak with the M1's SHA-3 instructions, and the paper does not separate the two effects. The repository's microbenchmarks and m1_benchmarks harnesses time only the optimised code; the reference rows of Tables 4-5 have no harness in the repo, while Table 6 reference rows can be reproduced through SUPERCOP 20210604 (README steps, first okcompilers line only). The microbenchmark Makefile builds with gcc -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer -march=native -mcpu=native. The repository was updated after publication (last commit 2024-11-10, PQClean namespacing and new compressions); the README says to use commit a96c17dbe74ac7675c785a728396e216555c432b to reproduce the paper. The LICENSE file offers MIT or CC0 1.0, and files without a header are CC0; vendored third-party files keep their own licences (Kyber and Dilithium reference code CC0 or Apache-2.0, Nguyen-Gaj Neon Kyber Apache-2.0 or public domain, feat.S MIT). CC0 has no patent grant. Cycle counts were read from the paper PDF (copy on the author's github.io repository), not re-run. The hand-written files are the __asm_NTT.S, __asm_iNTT.S, __asm_base_mul.S and __asm_poly.S sources in each scheme's ntt directory.

notes: All Dilithium ratios (4.15x, 4.12x, 5.98x, 5.15x, 8.6x, 1.44x, 2.12x, 1.63x) and the Kyber/Saber statements (1.7x, 2.1x, 9-14%, 26-41%, 2.0x) check out against the paper. Shortcomings to record: baseline is unoptimised reference C for Dilithium, Kyber/Saber gains only 1.1-2.1x over prior Neon code, full-scheme gains include faster Keccak, reference microbenchmark rows have no harness in the repo, repo changed after the paper (pinned commit a96c17d). Licence corrected to MIT OR CC0-1.0 per the current LICENSE file. Not a duplicate (pqm4 and PQRV in wave 13 target Cortex-M4 and RISC-V).

tier_reason: First-party README table (Xeon E3-1505M v6, 100 million iterations) against the rippled reference routines, with benchmark code in src/codec_hex.h, but no compiler version, an ambiguous build (build.sh g++ -O3 versus CMake clang Debug default), and a committed driver that cannot produce the table without edits; not raised to A.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated in the README and no compiler version anywhere. build.sh uses nasm -felf64 and g++ -std=c++14 -O3 (no -march or -mavx2, so the C reference is scalar); CMakeLists.txt instead defaults to clang with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE Debug plus -ggdb -fno-omit-frame-pointer. Which build produced the table is unknown.
corrections.caveats: The kernels are specialised to one fixed size (32 bytes, 64 hex digits) while the rippled baseline handles any length, so part of the gain comes from specialisation rather than assembly itself. The README's 'about 10x faster' is not matched by its own table (5.6x encode, 8.4x decode). Single machine, single run, the same constant input every iteration, no compiler version. The table cannot be reproduced from the committed code without edits: in the repository's only commit (2018-05-22) src/main.cpp returns right after test_base58(), so the hex benchmarks are unreachable, and build.sh does not assemble decode58.asm although codec_base58.h declares base58_8_coeff, while CMakeLists.txt defaults to a clang Debug build. The reference loops write to a local buffer that is never read, so an optimising compiler could shrink the C side (this would understate, not inflate, the assembly gain). The driver does random-test both kernels against the reference (1 million inputs, including invalid digits for the decoder), but the author calls the code a learning exercise that is 'not well tested'. No licence file, so reference only. The README also reports an AVX base58 coefficient routine gave only about 6% overall, and its 10x base58 gain over rippled (2199 ms versus 231 ms, 1 million iterations) is plain C++, not assembly.

notes: Numbers 1790/319 ms and 4694/561 ms and the CPU are on the README; ratios 5.6x and 8.4x are correct as derived. Shortcomings to record: README 10x overstated versus own table, fixed-size specialisation versus general baseline, committed main.cpp returns before the hex benchmark and build.sh is out of sync with the sources, no compiler version, no licence, single-commit learning project with 1 star. Kept at C; the record's suggestion of tier A is not supported.

tier_reason: Upgraded from D: an independent third-party benchmark (tana/pico_float_bench, public code float_bench.c, RP2040 at 125 MHz) times the Pico SDK float routines against an Arduino mbed core build that linked the GNU soft-float routines, but it is a single run with no compiler or flags, an unknown baseline clock and a whole-stack baseline, so numbers without full methodology stay at C; the SDK's own harness test/pico_float_test/float_benchmark.c publishes no results.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The SDK itself gives no numbers: its pico_float header says the RP2040 'pico' implementations, hand coded in the bootrom and the SDK, 'are generally faster and smaller than those provided by the C compiler/library'. Independent third-party benchmark tana/pico_float_bench (README results table, single measurement, 4000 Gaussian floats via Box-Muller on a Raspberry Pi Pico): Pico SDK build at 125 MHz 49 081 us generation, 11 560 us mean, 17 100 us variance, versus the Arduino mbed core build (which, per ArduinoCore-mbed issue #325, used the GNU floating point routines instead of the RP2040 ROM routines; clock not stated) at 248 237 us, 27 350 us and 36 410 us: 5.06x, 2.37x and 2.13x (derived from page data). No numbers for pico_mem_ops.
corrections.workload: Single-precision floating point arithmetic and math functions, and memcpy/memset, on RP2040. The SDK ships a cycle-level harness, test/pico_float_test/float_benchmark.c (and double_benchmark.c), built once per float implementation (compiler, pico, pico_vfp, pico_dcp) and timed with SysTick, but publishes no results. The third-party numbers come from tana/pico_float_bench float_bench.c: generate 4000 Gaussian floats with Box-Muller (rand, logf, sqrtf, cosf, sinf, plus one double multiply by M_PI), then compute a running mean and variance with float multiply, add and divide.
corrections.caveats: The SDK's own performance statement is qualitative; the RP2040 datasheet cycle tables were unreachable from this session (datasheets.raspberrypi.com did not resolve). The third-party comparison is a single measurement, states no compiler or flags, does not know the mbed core's clock (it cites ArduinoCore-mbed issue #221, F_CPU undefined), and compares whole software stacks (Pico SDK versus the RTOS-based Arduino mbed core), not only the float routines. ArduinoCore-mbed issue #325 (mbed core placed GNU float routines in RAM instead of using the ROM routines) was closed as completed on 2021-11-08 after a patch, although the benchmark README says the situation was similar in November 2023; when the 248 ms row was measured is not stated. The workload multiplies by M_PI in double precision, so it also exercises double routines. Part of the RP2040 float code lives in the chip bootrom (the header says 'from the bootrom and the SDK'), not in this SDK alone, and the routines do not support all features of a fully compliant IEEE implementation. On RP2350 the SDK uses VFP or DCP hardware instead. No numbers were found for pico_mem_ops.

notes: Record said the repo has no benchmark for these routines; it does (test/pico_float_test/float_benchmark.c, per-implementation SysTick timing) but publishes no results. Found independent numbers in tana/pico_float_bench (5.06x generation, 2.37x mean, 2.13x variance, derived) and raised the tier from D to C. Shortcomings to record: whole-stack baseline with unknown clock, single run, no compiler or flags, part of the code is in the RP2040 bootrom, not fully IEEE compliant, no numbers for pico_mem_ops.
